title: Mapwork: the skills of the extract

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Everything a map extract asks: grid references, directions and bearings, distances, heights and cross-sections, the key, and reading the landscape from the evidence, relief, drainage, settlement, communications and land use.

blocks.heading: Grid references
blocks.text: A map is divided into squares by eastings, the vertical lines numbered west to east, and northings, the horizontal lines numbered south to north. A four-figure reference names a whole square by the lines at its bottom-left corner: square 4664 is the square whose corner is easting 46 and northing 64. A six-figure reference locates a point inside the square by adding a third figure to each pair: the tenths of the way across, then the tenths of the way up. The order is fixed, eastings first, then northings, along the corridor, then up the stairs, and the figures come from the grid lines, never from road numbers or other labels on the sheet. A point halfway across square 4664 and three-tenths up is 465463: the easting 46 becomes 465, the northing 64 becomes 643.

blocks.heading: Directions and bearings
blocks.text: A compass direction is a point of the compass, given as the direction of one place from another: north-north-east, south-west, east. A bearing is different: an angle measured clockwise from grid north, in degrees, so east is 090, south is 180 and west is 270. A bearing of 135 is south-east; the two answers name the same direction in different systems, and a question asks for one or the other by name. Bearings are measured clockwise from grid north with a protractor, its centre on the starting point and its zero line along grid north.

blocks.heading: Distances along a route
blocks.text: To measure a straight-line distance, lay the paper's edge between the two points, mark both, and set the marks against the scale line. To measure a distance along a route, a road, a river, a path, follow the route with the straight edge of a sheet of paper, marking each bend on the paper as you go, then lay the whole chain of marks on the scale line and read the total. A straight-line measurement between the ends underestimates a winding route, sometimes badly. On a 1:50 000 map, 1 centimetre on the map is 0.5 kilometres on the ground; on a 1:25 000 map, 1 centimetre is 0.25 kilometres. A route measuring 6.4 centimetres on the 1:50 000 sheet is 6.4 x 0.5 = 3.2 kilometres on the ground.

blocks.heading: Heights from contours
blocks.text: Contours join points of equal height, shown on most extracts every 10 metres. Read them in three ways. The height of a place is the contour it sits on or between, or the spot height printed at the point, which is exact where the contour is approximate. The difference in height between two places is the highest contour crossed minus the lowest: from the 40-metre contour to the 120-metre contour is 120 - 40 = 80 metres of climb. The spacing of the contours gives the steepness: bunched contours mean a steep slope, widely spaced ones a gentle one, and a cluster of contours close together against a contour far apart marks a cliff. A triangulation pillar marks a surveyed high point.

blocks.heading: Cross-sections
blocks.text: A cross-section shows the shape of the land along a line drawn on the map. Draw the line, mark every contour it crosses, and plot each crossing against distance and height on a grid: the line joining the plotted points is the profile of the slope. The vertical scale is usually drawn larger than the horizontal scale to make the shape readable, which is vertical exaggeration, and the exaggeration should be stated so the reader knows the slopes look steeper than they are. A section that rises in steps is a gentle slope becoming a steep one; a section with a broad low flat stretch between two rises is a valley with a flood plain in the middle.

blocks.heading: Translating the scale
blocks.text: A feature's real size is its map measurement multiplied by the scale. On a 1:50 000 map, a wood measuring 3 centimetres across is 3 x 0.5 = 1.5 kilometres wide on the ground; a 4-centimetre stretch of coast on a 1:25 000 sheet is 4 x 0.25 = 1 kilometre. The same conversion turns a real distance into a map distance for planning: 2 kilometres on the ground is 2 / 0.5 = 4 centimetres on the 1:50 000 sheet. Describing a feature in real terms, the width of the estuary, the length of the ridge, is this multiplication, and the answer carries its unit, kilometres.

blocks.heading: The key
blocks.text: The key is read before the map, because the symbols are the map's vocabulary. Each symbol carries a precise category: the key says national road, not highway; coniferous plantation, not trees; nonconiferous woodland, not wood. An answer that names a feature with the key's own term is right, and a general term is not. The symbols carry more than names: the width of a road symbol shows the road's importance, the style of a building symbol shows its use, a school, a church, a hospital, and the colour of an area shows its cover, blue for water, green for woodland, white for open ground.

blocks.heading: Drawing inferences from the map
blocks.text: A map is evidence, and the skill is to draw what it supports. Settlements cluster where the land is flat and water is near, so a line of villages along a valley floor is no accident; roads avoid the steepest gradients, so a main road that bends round a spur is taking the gentle way; land use follows the relief, so the rough grazing sits on the steep slopes and the arable fields on the flat. Every inference is drawn from stated evidence, the feature read from the map, the pattern it makes, and the conclusion the pattern supports, and an inference that names no evidence is a guess.

blocks.heading: Describing landscape features
blocks.text: A landscape description names the features and their character with geographical terms and simple adjectives: a wide flat-floored valley, a steep convex slope, a rocky headland, a nucleated village on the valley floor. The terms are the syllabus's own, the adjectives are simple, and together they say what the landscape is like without explaining it. Relief is the height and shape of the land; drainage is the water on it, the rivers and streams, their pattern, density and flow direction; the two are described separately, and a drainage feature that is not on the map cannot be described from it.

blocks.heading: Drainage and the relief
blocks.text: Drainage density is the length of stream channels per unit area. A wet upland carries closely spaced streams between bunched contours, high density; a dry lowland carries a few streams in wide valleys, low density. Stream patterns read from the shape of their joining: a dendritic pattern, branches like a tree, suits uniform rock; streams bending round parallel spurs mark a valley side; a stream flowing between two spurs sits in the syncline the contours draw. The flow direction comes from the heights: water flows from the high ground to the low, so the contours at the stream's two ends settle which way it runs.

blocks.heading: Coastlines and river channels
blocks.text: On a large-scale map a coastline reads three ways: cliffs show as a hard edge with contours bunched against it, a beach as a flat strip at sea level beside the low-water mark, and a marsh as flat ground with the wet symbols, reeds or tidal marks. A river channel changes downstream: a narrow, straight channel in the upper square, meanders and a broader channel in the middle, and a wide mouth with marsh in the last, because the discharge grows as tributaries join.

blocks.heading: Land use
blocks.text: Land use follows the land. Improved pasture and arable fields sit on the flat lowland where the ground can be ploughed; rough grazing climbs the slopes that machinery cannot; woodland clothes the steepest ground, where nothing else pays; settlement strings along the main routes. The map shows the pattern, the field shapes large and rectangular on the planned lowland, small and irregular on the old common land, and the inference comes from matching the use to the relief that suits it.

blocks.heading: Settlement patterns
blocks.text: Settlements sit in three patterns. Nucleated: the buildings grouped round a centre, a church, a green, a junction, the old defensive and market shape. Linear: the buildings strung along a line, a road or a valley floor, each house taking its frontage from the route. Dispersed: farms scattered across the area with no centre, the pattern of enclosure country where each holding stands on its own land. The pattern is described from the map, and its reason inferred: nucleation suits a village with a church and services, linear suits a route through enclosed ground, dispersal suits large farms worked from the homestead.

blocks.heading: Urban morphology
blocks.text: A town's shape reads on the large-scale sheet in zones. At the centre, a dense grid of tightly packed blocks, the commercial heart, with the market square, the chain stores and the offices. Around it, terraced streets and semi-detached rows, the nineteenth-century growth, small regular plots along straight streets. At the edge, detached housing with gardens and the post-war estates, where the streets curve and the plots widen, and beyond them the retail park and the bypass, the newest growth with its car parks. Reading the zones is reading the town's history, and the pattern of one zone into the next is the urban morphology the map shows.

blocks.heading: Functions, services, site and growth
blocks.text: A settlement's function is what it does, its main economic and social activities: a port town with docks and warehouses, a market town with a livestock market and a coaching inn, a resort with a promenade and a golf course. Its services are what it provides, the school, the hospital, the college, and the two together tell the region what the settlement is for. The site, the land the town stands on, was chosen for what it offered: dry flat ground, a water supply, a bridging point, a sheltered harbour or a defensive spur. Growth then followed the routes and the work: the town on the bridging point grew where the roads converged on its bridge.

blocks.heading: Communication networks
blocks.text: Communications are read in type and density. Type: motorway, dual carriageway, main road, minor road, track, mainline railway, branch line, navigable river, each with its own symbol and its own speed. Density: how close the routes stand, thick on the lowland where the settlement is dense, thin in the upland where each valley carries one road. The network follows the land, because routes take the cheapest gradient: the motorway runs along the flat, the minor road threads the valley, and the paths cross the ridge at the saddle where the climb is least.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: Every theme of Papers 1 and 4 arrives on Paper 2 as a resource: population as pyramids and densities, rivers as channel shapes and drainage patterns, settlements as morphology and function, development as data to plot. The skills here are the toolkit, and the four map extracts used in the cards are the practice ground.
